items.title: Structures inside the testis
items.guide: Identify seminiferous tubules as sites of sperm development. Sertoli cells inside them support developing germ cells. Interstitial cells between tubules produce testosterone. Keep a sperm cell separate from the tissues that support it.
items.bindingReview: Tubules house germ cells, Sertoli support within and Leydig hormones between; different compartments.

items.title: Match production sites
items.guide: Testosterone: mainly testicular interstitial cells. Progesterone: corpus luteum, and later the placenta during pregnancy. Sperm: seminiferous tubules. LH and FSH: anterior pituitary. The oocyte develops in an ovarian follicle; the ovulated cell usually completes meiosis II only after sperm entry.
items.bindingReview: All six sites matched; ovulated secondary oocyte distinguished from a completed ovum and luteal/placental hormone timing retained. Route-order rereview: required links precede this chapter practice. Later explanations are optional further reading; necessary extension context is visible before attempt.
items.furtherReadingPolicy: Later optional follow-up; never represented as a previously completed prerequisite.
items.preAttemptContext: Before this optional reinforcement, distinguish a hormone’s source from its target. The corpus luteum makes progesterone after ovulation; during pregnancy the placenta later becomes a major progesterone source. The later pregnancy lesson explains that transition.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Trace the sperm pathway
items.guide: Trace seminiferous tubules → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra → vagina → cervix → uterus → uterine tube. Label maturation at the epididymis and the usual fertilization site in a uterine tube. The pathway is more than a list: each arrow means movement.
items.bindingReview: Duct sequence independently traced through both tracts; no bladder, ovary or endometrium inserted into sperm route. Route-order rereview: required links precede this chapter practice. Later explanations are optional further reading; necessary extension context is visible before attempt.
items.furtherReadingPolicy: Later optional follow-up; never represented as a previously completed prerequisite.

items.title: Explain semen components
items.guide: Semen contains sperm plus glandular fluids. Seminal-vesicle fluid contributes nutrients and much of the volume; prostate fluid contributes enzymes and other substances; Cowper gland mucus contributes lubrication. Sperm carry genetic information. These glands support delivery and the chemical environment; they do not make sperm.
items.bindingReview: Three accessory fluids have distinct contributions; none manufactures sperm.

items.title: Sequence follicle development
items.guide: A developing oocyte is enclosed by follicular support cells. FSH supports follicle growth and estrogen production. A selected mature follicle responds to the LH surge and releases a secondary oocyte. The remaining follicular tissue becomes the corpus luteum. Without pregnancy support, it regresses; the oocyte is never the corpus luteum.
items.bindingReview: Follicle support cells and released oocyte separated; FSH growth then LH ovulation then residual luteal tissue.

items.title: Describe endometrial changes
items.guide: Menstruation sheds much of the functional lining after ovarian steroid levels fall. Estrogen supports rebuilding during the proliferative phase. After ovulation, progesterone supports a secretory lining suited to implantation. If the corpus luteum regresses, progesterone and estrogen decline and a new menstrual phase begins.
items.bindingReview: Withdrawal shedding, estrogen rebuilding and progesterone secretory support occur in that order.

items.title: Read the hormone graph
items.guide: The sharp red mid-cycle peak is the best match for LH. The dashed curve that rises after that peak is progesterone; it is the main answer to the later-half increase. Identify curves by timing and shape. The printed introduction says four hormones, but this graph visibly supplies only three curves; do not invent a fourth.
items.bindingReview: Rechecked source image: LH is the sharp red mid-cycle peak and progesterone the dashed post-peak curve; source claims four hormones but shows three.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: The introduction names four hormones, but the supplied graph shows three curves. Interpret only visible labelled evidence.

items.title: Predict an acrosome defect
items.guide: The acrosome supports sperm interaction with and penetration of the oocyte’s coverings. Without it, ordinary fertilization would be strongly impaired even if sperm could move. Name the affected step; the case does not show that sperm production or every possible assisted method is absent.
items.bindingReview: Acrosome impairment affects interaction with coverings, not necessarily movement or sperm formation. Route-order rereview: required links precede this chapter practice. Later explanations are optional further reading; necessary extension context is visible before attempt.
items.furtherReadingPolicy: Later optional follow-up; never represented as a previously completed prerequisite.

items.title: Use feedback in an animal case
items.guide: Removing testes removes sperm-producing tissues and the main typical testosterone source. Reduced androgen action may reduce some androgen-dependent traits and sexual or aggressive behaviour, with species, age and conditions affecting the outcome. Reduced testosterone feedback can permit greater gonadotropin release. For a farmer, preventing unwanted breeding and sometimes easier handling can be advantages; these are separate from animal-welfare costs, and calmer behaviour is not guaranteed.
items.bindingReview: Source asks farm advantages too: preventing breeding and possible easier handling added with behavioural uncertainty and welfare distinction.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Removing testes removes a major source of testosterone and sperm production. Reduced testosterone can change androgen-dependent traits and behaviour, with species, age and context affecting the result. Reduced negative feedback may increase upstream gonadotropin release. Agricultural benefits and welfare costs must be evaluated separately; no single behavioural outcome is guaranteed.

items.title: Plan a cycle investigation
items.guide: Two possible model explanations are reduced pituitary stimulation of ovarian tissue or a reduced ovarian response despite adequate stimulation. Compare synthetic repeated FSH/LH and ovarian-steroid measurements with a reference cycle, using the same method and sampling intervals. Predict lower upstream signals in the first model and potentially maintained or increased upstream signals with weak ovarian steroid output in the second. Repeated timing and target-response evidence would help distinguish them. The pattern alone cannot diagnose a person or select treatment.
items.bindingReview: Two candidate mechanisms now generate different measurable signal/response predictions; method and sampling interval controlled.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Several mechanisms could alter a cycle, including altered upstream signals, ovarian responses or feedback. Choose one fictional mechanism, specify observations of hormone patterns over time, and hold the measurement method constant. A classroom plan uses supplied data; an irregular cycle alone cannot identify a diagnosis or justify an intervention.

items.title: Separate chromosome, hormone and receptor evidence
items.guide: Under the simplified XX developmental pathway, ovaries would be expected, but chromosomes alone do not establish every anatomical feature. Cells lacking functional estrogen receptors cannot produce the usual response to estrogen. Adrenal androgens do not prove a particular set of traits. Reproductive function could be disrupted, but these facts cannot establish an individual’s fertility.
items.bindingReview: XX typical gonad expectation is distinct from receptor response, and chromosomes or adrenal androgen alone cannot determine traits or fertility.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Treat this as a fictional signalling model. Chromosomes, hormone concentrations and receptor responses do not individually determine every trait or outcome.

items.title: Explain pregnancy and menstrual suppression
items.guide: Early trophoblast hCG maintains the corpus luteum, sustaining progesterone and estrogen; the placenta later becomes a major hormone source. Endometrial support prevents the usual withdrawal-related menstruation. After placental delivery these hormone sources change. Ovulatory cycles return at variable times, particularly during lactation; postpartum bleeding is not automatically menstruation.
items.bindingReview: hCG sustains luteal steroids early; placental delivery changes support later. Timing of ovulatory return and postpartum bleeding qualified. Route-order rereview: required links precede this chapter practice. Later explanations are optional further reading; necessary extension context is visible before attempt.
items.furtherReadingPolicy: Later optional follow-up; never represented as a previously completed prerequisite.
items.preAttemptContext: Optional pregnancy background: trophoblast is an outer cell population of the early conceptus. Its hCG signal supports the corpus luteum, maintaining progesterone and estrogen until placental hormone production is established. These hormones maintain uterine support. Placental delivery changes hormone sources; ovulatory cycles return at variable times, and lactation can delay their return. Postpartum bleeding is not automatically menstruation.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Connect development, growth and differentiation
items.guide: Development is the overall sequence of changes. Growth increases size or cell number; differentiation makes cells functionally specialized. Early cleavage increases cell number without increasing total conceptus size. Later development combines growth, movement and specialization to form tissues and organs.
items.bindingReview: Growth, specialization and form distinguished; cleavage partitions cells before substantial overall growth.

items.title: Sequence fertilization
items.guide: Sperm reach a uterine tube and undergo changes that allow interaction with the oocyte’s coverings. Membranes fuse; the oocyte completes meiosis II and activates mechanisms limiting additional sperm entry. Parental chromosome sets combine in the new diploid lineage. Cleavage then begins. Distinguish fertilization from later implantation.
items.bindingReview: Transport/readiness, covering interaction, fusion, meiotic completion/block and diploid lineage precede cleavage.

items.title: Compare morula and blastocyst
items.guide: A morula is a compact cluster of early cells. A blastocyst has a fluid-filled cavity, an inner cell mass and an outer trophoblast layer. The distinction is organization as well as cell number; the blastocyst is the stage involved in implantation.
items.bindingReview: Morula compactness versus blastocyst cavity and two cell populations directly answers structural comparison.

items.title: Compare inner cell mass and trophoblast
items.guide: The inner cell mass gives rise to the embryo and some associated tissues. The trophoblast interacts with the endometrium, produces early hCG and contributes to the fetal part of the placenta. Neither label means that the whole placenta is made from one source: maternal tissue also contributes.
items.bindingReview: Inner mass and trophoblast distinguished without assigning the whole placenta to one fetal source.

items.title: Explain hCG
items.guide: Early trophoblast-derived hCG acts on the corpus luteum to maintain ovarian progesterone and estrogen secretion. This supports the endometrium until placental hormone production is established. hCG is a signal, not the embryo’s nutrient supply, and its presence alone does not describe every aspect of development.
items.bindingReview: Signal source and corpus-luteum target linked to steroid maintenance rather than nutrient delivery.

items.title: Connect germ layers to organs
items.guide: Ectoderm contributes to epidermis, brain and spinal cord. Endoderm contributes to digestive lining, respiratory lining and much of the liver/pancreatic epithelial tissue. Mesoderm contributes to muscle, skeleton and reproductive structures. Many organs contain tissues from several layers; not every endocrine gland has an endodermal origin.
items.bindingReview: Three ectoderm examples, three endoderm-derived epithelial examples and three mesoderm examples; mixed organ origins qualified.

items.title: Explain placental formation and functions
items.guide: Chorionic tissue from the conceptus forms close exchange surfaces with the uterine endometrium. Maternal and fetal blood normally remain in separate circulations. Gases, nutrients and wastes cross the interface; the placenta also produces hormones. It supports exchange and signalling, but it is not an absolute barrier to every agent.
items.bindingReview: Maternal and fetal contributions, separate circulation, exchange and endocrine functions all included.

items.title: Distinguish chorion and amnion
items.guide: The amnion surrounds the fluid-filled space around the developing embryo/fetus. The chorion is an outer extraembryonic membrane that contributes to the fetal portion of the placenta. Connect each membrane to its location and function; neither is the same as the uterine lining.
items.bindingReview: Amnion surrounds fluid; chorion contributes outer fetal placental tissue; neither is endometrium.

items.title: Explain amniotic fluid
items.guide: Amniotic fluid cushions movement and provides a protected physical environment in which the fetus can move and develop. The fluid-filled space and its membrane differ from the placental blood-exchange interface. Oxygen from maternal blood reaches fetal blood mainly through placental exchange; amniotic fluid is not a direct maternal-blood supply.
items.bindingReview: Protection and movement answer fluid function; blood-gas exchange stays placental. Untaught lung-specific claim removed.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Amniotic fluid cushions movement, helps maintain a protected physical environment and permits fetal movement. It contributes to normal development, including lung development. It is not the main route for delivering oxygen from maternal blood; that occurs through placental exchange and fetal circulation.

items.title: Relate yolk sac and allantois
items.guide: In humans, the yolk sac supports early blood-cell formation and contributes to early gut and germ-cell development; it is not a large yolk food store like a bird’s. The allantois is an early outgrowth associated with the connecting stalk and later urinary/umbilical development. Distinguish human functions from those in shelled eggs.
items.bindingReview: Human roles compared rather than copying bird yolk/waste roles; short optional background precedes attempt.
items.preAttemptContext: Optional background for the species comparison: the human yolk sac is associated with early blood formation, the early gut and the germ-cell pathway. It is not a large store of yolk. A human allantois has relationships to early connecting-stalk and urinary development.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Compare developmental periods
items.guide: Five embryonic changes are implantation, formation of three germ layers, neural-tube formation, early heart/blood-vessel development, and limb/organ patterning. Five fetal changes are increasing body size, continuing skeletal development, increasingly coordinated movement, nervous-system maturation, and lung maturation. These changes overlap. The fetal period begins after roughly eight weeks measured from fertilization, about ten weeks on a typical last-menstrual-period clock; the organs are not all mature at that boundary.
items.bindingReview: Counted five distinct embryonic and five fetal changes; developmental clock and overlapping events explicit.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: An embryonic sequence includes implantation, gastrulation, neural-tube development, early heart/circulatory development and limb/organ patterning. The fetal period emphasizes growth, skeletal development, movement, nervous-system maturation and lung maturation. Use approximate overlapping stages; specify that the embryonic/fetal boundary near eight weeks is measured from fertilization, not from the last menstrual period.

items.title: Define morphogenesis
items.guide: Morphogenesis is the development of biological form through coordinated cell division, movement, shape change and organization. It includes arranging tissues into structures. Growth alone does not explain form, and differentiation alone does not explain where tissues are positioned.
items.bindingReview: Form involves arrangement, movement and shape, not size increase alone.

items.title: Explain labour control
items.guide: Progesterone action helps keep the pregnant uterus relatively quiet. Human labour involves a reduced calming action and greater response to contraction-promoting signals; a large fall in circulating progesterone before labour is not required. Prostaglandins support cervical change and contractions. Cervical stretch can reinforce oxytocin release and stronger contractions. The broad stages are cervical dilation, delivery of the fetus, then placental separation and delivery. Birth removes the major stretch stimulus from this feedback model.
items.bindingReview: Corrected progesterone-action model retained and missing three delivery stages added.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: For humans, distinguish functional changes in progesterone signalling from a required major decline in its circulating concentration.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Progesterone action helps maintain a relatively quiet uterus. Human labour involves a shift away from that calming action alongside greater responsiveness to contraction-promoting signals; it does not require a large fall in circulating progesterone before labour. Prostaglandins and oxytocin promote contractions, cervical stretch can reinforce the loop, birth removes the stretch stimulus, and the placenta is delivered.

items.title: Explain an exposure pathway
items.guide: Some agents in maternal circulation can cross placental exchange tissues into fetal circulation. Their transfer and effects depend on chemical properties, amount, timing and metabolism. The placenta separates blood compartments but does not block every substance. The pathway explains a possibility, not an individual developmental prediction.
items.bindingReview: Material crosses tissue interface from maternal to fetal circulation; does not imply open blood continuity or universal harmful effect.

items.title: Evaluate environmental influences
items.guide: Two beneficial examples are varied adequate nutrition, which provides materials for growth, and prenatal health support, which can help identify nutritional or exposure concerns. Two detrimental exposures are alcohol, which can affect developing tissues including the nervous system, and tobacco smoke, whose components can impair oxygen delivery and growth. Amount, timing and other conditions influence the outcome. These are population-level biological examples, not a prediction about an individual or a reason for blame.
items.bindingReview: Two beneficial and two harmful examples with mechanisms now explicit, provided in optional background before this reinforcement task.
items.preAttemptContext: Optional background for this textbook task: adequate nutrition supplies materials used in development, and prenatal health support can identify nutritional or exposure concerns. Alcohol can affect developing nervous tissue; components of tobacco smoke can affect oxygen delivery and growth. Outcomes depend on exposure and context.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Use evidence-based examples such as adequate nutrition and appropriate prenatal health support, contrasted with exposure to alcohol or tobacco smoke. Explain the biological pathway and developmental timing. Avoid blaming an individual or claiming that one behaviour guarantees an outcome; medication decisions cannot be inferred from a school model.

items.title: Build a hormone relationship table
items.guide: A five-row table can show: early trophoblast → hCG → corpus luteum → continued steroid support; corpus luteum and later placenta → progesterone → endometrium/uterine tissue → pregnancy support; ovarian follicles and later placental production → estrogen → responsive reproductive tissues → growth and changing responsiveness; hypothalamic neurons, released by posterior pituitary → oxytocin → uterus and mammary contractile cells → contractions and milk ejection; anterior pituitary → prolactin → milk-producing mammary cells → milk synthesis. Sources and timing change; synthesis and ejection are different actions.
items.bindingReview: Five hormones now include actual sources, targets and actions; oxytocin synthesis versus release sites separated.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: A valid set is hCG → corpus-luteum support; progesterone → endometrial/pregnancy support; estrogen → tissue growth and changing reproductive responsiveness; oxytocin → uterine contractions and milk ejection; prolactin → milk synthesis. Include sources, targets and timing, and show that synthesis and release of milk are different actions.

items.title: Distinguish synthesis from release
items.guide: The intended synthesis pathway is reduced prolactin secretion or action, which could reduce ongoing milk production. Oxytocin mainly controls milk ejection. A drug description alone does not prove its molecular mechanism, so state the predicted pathway rather than identifying or recommending a medicine.
items.bindingReview: Synthesis requires prolactin pathway; ejection uses oxytocin, and a drug description cannot establish molecular action.

items.title: Explain why sperm number can matter
items.guide: Many sperm do not reach or successfully interact with the oocyte, so number, movement, structure and transport can affect probability. A lower count may reduce the chance that a suitable sperm arrives. The printed ten-million cutoff is not a sufficient modern infertility diagnosis; retain the probability mechanism and remove the categorical diagnosis.
items.bindingReview: Probability of a suitable sperm reaching the oocyte explains numbers; historical threshold is not a diagnosis.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Use sperm number as one probabilistic factor. The printed threshold is not a sufficient contemporary infertility diagnosis.

items.title: Predict a gonadotropin effect
items.guide: GnRH normally stimulates pituitary FSH and LH. Under some fertility-treatment conditions, increased ovarian stimulation can allow more than one follicle/oocyte to mature, increasing the possibility of multiple fertilizations. This is a mechanism-level possibility; outcomes depend on the treatment and response, and the question is not a treatment recommendation.
items.bindingReview: GnRH–pituitary–ovarian pathway can stimulate multiple follicles in the stated treatment model; no universal effect or regimen inferred.

items.title: Model the origin of twins
items.guide: Show one fertilized egg forming an early embryo that splits into two developing embryos, compared with two eggs fertilized separately. Correct the source’s claim that identical twins always share one chorion/placenta: membrane arrangements depend on development and may be separate or shared. Shared zygote origin does not mean every later trait or mutation is identical.
items.bindingReview: One embryo splitting versus two fertilizations; chorion/placenta arrangement not universal or guaranteed identical later phenotype.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Monozygotic twins do not invariably share one chorion or placenta. Membrane arrangements vary.

items.title: Reproduction and survival
items.guide: Reproduction supports continuity across generations and is not required for one person’s immediate survival in the way gas exchange is. Reproductive organs and hormones also have functions affecting health. Avoid implying that an individual must reproduce or that one system is biologically unimportant.
items.bindingReview: Species continuity distinguished from immediate individual survival and health functions; no claim an individual must reproduce.

items.title: Compare reproductive systems
items.guide: Three similarities are production of haploid gametes, supporting tissues for developing germ cells, and pituitary–gonadal hormone regulation. Three differences are: typical sperm production yields four spermatids per primary spermatocyte while oogenesis concentrates cytoplasm in one larger cell; sperm mature in the epididymis and move through the vas/urethra while oocytes move through uterine tubes; and a receptive uterus supports implantation and prenatal development, a function absent from the male tract. Compare a named process on each side.
items.bindingReview: Counted three specific similarities and three matched differences rather than a vague list of two systems.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Both systems produce gametes, provide supporting tissues and respond to hormonal control. Typical differences include sperm versus oocyte production patterns, transport structures and support for internal development. State the particular structure or process being compared; a broad label does not substitute for a mechanism.

items.title: Compare gametes
items.guide: Both normally carry one chromosome set and contribute genetic information. Sperm are small, have an acrosome and flagellum, and are specialized for movement and delivery. An oocyte retains much more cytoplasm and cellular resources. Formation differs in timing and division pattern, but both involve meiosis.
items.bindingReview: Shared haploid role and different cytoplasm/movement/timing; no claim same allele sequence.

items.title: Identify germ layers
items.guide: Ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm become established in the embryonic disc during gastrulation, as cells move and reorganize. This produces a trilaminar embryonic disc, meaning a disc with three germ layers. The layers are developing cell populations, not three separate fully formed organs.
items.bindingReview: Source explicitly asks cellular body: embryonic disc now named and introduced before the optional attempt.
items.preAttemptContext: The embryonic disc is a flattened early embryonic structure. Trilaminar means having three layers. Use these terms to describe the germ layers established during gastrulation.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm are established during gastrulation as cells reorganize into a three-layered embryonic structure. They do not first appear as three separate fully formed organs. Connect gastrulation to later differentiation.

items.title: Explain a complete cycle
items.guide: Link follicular growth and estrogen to endometrial rebuilding, sustained high estrogen to an LH surge, ovulation to formation of the corpus luteum, and progesterone to a secretory lining. Without continuing luteal support, steroid levels fall and menstruation occurs. Keep ovarian and uterine events on distinct but coordinated tracks.
items.bindingReview: Both ovarian and uterine tracks plus changing feedback represented.

items.title: Distinguish testicular structures
items.guide: Seminiferous tubules contain the developing sperm lineage. Sertoli cells within them support that lineage. Interstitial cells between tubules produce testosterone. In the sketch, show locations and functions, not three interchangeable labels for sperm.
items.bindingReview: Three tissue labels and spatial locations consistent with source sketch request.

items.title: Connect semen to its sources
items.guide: Sperm from seminiferous tubules join secretions from seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper glands. Seminal-vesicle fluid contributes nutrients and much of the volume, prostate fluid contributes enzymes and other substances, and Cowper mucus lubricates the passage. The resulting semen is usually slightly alkaline and helps buffer the acidic vaginal environment during delivery. The secretions differ; do not give every gland the same pH or imply that buffering guarantees sperm survival or fertilization.
items.bindingReview: Acidity buffering mechanism now answers part c, with distinct gland secretions and no guaranteed fertilization.
items.preAttemptContext: A buffer reduces changes in acidity. Semen is usually slightly alkaline; the vaginal environment is usually acidic. Secretions from different glands need not have identical acidity or composition.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Sperm arise from seminiferous tubules and join secretions from seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper glands. The combined fluid supports transport and the chemical environment, including buffering. Individual secretions differ; the phrase “mainly alkaline” describes the mixture, not an identical function for each gland.

items.title: Read the labelled anatomy
items.guide: Male diagram: A vas deferens; B urethra; C penis; D epididymis; E testis; F scrotum; G seminal vesicle; H prostate. Female diagram: I uterine/Fallopian tube; J ovary; K uterus; L cervix; M vagina. Check each leader line against the supplied page, not only nearby structures.
items.bindingReview: A–M leader-line mappings verified against original image; all thirteen structures retained.

items.title: Explain the labelled anatomy
items.guide: A transports sperm; B carries semen/urine at different times; C supports delivery; D supports maturation/storage; E produces sperm and hormones; F helps regulate the testicular environment; G and H add seminal fluid. I transports the oocyte and is the usual fertilization region; J supports oocytes and hormone secretion; K supports implantation/development; L is the uterine opening; M is the canal to the exterior.
items.bindingReview: All thirteen functions linked to the same structure key; urethral dual use at different times, uterus versus tube distinguished.

items.title: Hormones and sex characteristics
items.guide: GnRH stimulates FSH/LH release; these act on gonads. Gonadal steroids influence reproductive organs and secondary characteristics during development/puberty. Name a source, hormone, target and response. A hormone acts where receptors and the appropriate developmental context are present; it does not act identically on every cell.
items.bindingReview: Upstream hormones and responsive gonadal/other targets cover both primary and secondary traits.

items.title: Match ovarian hormone roles
items.guide: a estrogen; b estrogen in the simplified pubertal context; c progesterone; d progesterone and estrogen; e LH; f estrogen; g FSH. For h, progesterone and estrogen can contribute negative feedback, but estrogen’s effect depends on sustained level and cycle stage. No rule says every high estrogen level always inhibits GnRH.
items.bindingReview: Eight lettered matches checked; h is context-dependent estrogen/progesterone feedback, not permanent estrogen inhibition.

items.title: Explain male feedback
items.guide: GnRH supports pituitary FSH/LH release. FSH acts through Sertoli cells; LH promotes interstitial-cell testosterone production. Testosterone provides negative feedback to upstream centres, and inhibin particularly limits FSH. Predict a change through the pathway rather than drawing every arrow as stimulation.
items.bindingReview: Testosterone feedback and inhibin/FSH control kept distinct; both source and response supported.

items.title: Separate blastocyst cell groups
items.guide: The inner cell mass contributes to the embryo and associated tissues. Trophoblast participates in implantation, early hormone signalling and the fetal part of the placenta. Maternal tissue also contributes to placental structure.
items.bindingReview: Both cell groups and maternal placental contribution distinguished.

items.title: Give germ-layer examples
items.guide: Ectoderm: epidermis and nervous system. Mesoderm: skeletal muscle and skeleton. Endoderm: digestive and respiratory epithelial linings. Additional accurate examples may be used, but whole organs often contain more than one tissue origin.
items.bindingReview: Two examples per layer named without claiming every component of each organ shares one origin.

items.title: Explain extraembryonic support
items.guide: Amnion encloses amniotic fluid; chorion contributes to the fetal placental interface; yolk sac has early blood/gut-related roles; allantois contributes to early connecting-stalk/urinary development. The placenta is an exchange and endocrine organ formed with maternal and fetal contributions. Distinguish these human roles from a bird egg’s large yolk store.
items.bindingReview: Four extraembryonic structures and maternal/fetal placental interface named by human function.

items.title: Locate spermatogenesis
items.guide: Seminiferous tubules provide the organized site where germ cells develop through spermatogenesis with Sertoli-cell support. They are distinct from the testosterone-producing interstitial cells and the epididymis where later maturation/storage occurs.
items.bindingReview: Production site distinguished from interstitial endocrine and epididymal maturation locations.

items.title: Explain the acrosome
items.guide: The acrosome is a specialized cap of the sperm head. Its contents and membrane changes contribute to interaction with the oocyte’s coverings. It is not a structure that produces the sperm’s chromosomes or its flagellum.
items.bindingReview: Male sperm-head structure, covering interaction rather than flagellum/chromosome production.

items.title: Explain the polyspermy block
items.guide: After sperm–oocyte membrane interaction, activation of the oocyte triggers changes including cortical-granule release and modification of the surrounding zona pellucida, reducing further sperm entry. Do not import a sea-urchin electrical “fast block” as the required human mechanism.
items.bindingReview: Human cortical-granule/zona change; avoids the sea-urchin fast electrical block.

items.title: Compare prevention goals
items.guide: Avoiding the sexual contact that transmits pathogens prevents that route of transmission and conception; correctly used external or internal condoms can reduce risks of both conception and many STIs. Protection is not absolute, especially for exposed skin. Hormonal contraception alone does not prevent STI transmission.
items.bindingReview: Barrier and avoiding transmission contact are different methods; hormonal signalling alone does not prevent STIs. Optional context supplies this scope.
items.preAttemptContext: Optional background: an external or internal condom forms a physical barrier that reduces contact and movement of fluids. Some pathogens can also spread through uncovered skin. Hormonal methods change reproductive signalling; they do not themselves block pathogen transmission. Avoiding the contact responsible for a transmission route removes that particular route.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Compare early stages
items.guide: A morula is a compact cell mass; a blastocyst has a cavity plus distinct inner-cell-mass and trophoblast regions. The latter organization supports implantation. Neither stage is a fully formed miniature fetus.
items.bindingReview: Organization and implantation-ready stage distinguished from mere cell count.

items.title: Distinguish ovulation from uterine support
items.guide: Natural menopause generally ends ovarian ovulation. That does not mean the uterus can never support development: assisted reproduction with an embryo and appropriate medical support may be possible in some circumstances. The question needs this distinction, not an absolute yes/no fertility prediction.
items.bindingReview: Loss of ovarian ovulation does not logically imply every possible uterine-support route fails; no fertility guarantee.

items.title: Explain mammary development
items.guide: Estrogen, progesterone and prolactin contribute to mammary development and preparation. After birth, changing steroid levels permit prolactin-supported milk synthesis, while oxytocin mediates ejection. A preparation question and a milk-release question ask about different parts of the pathway.
items.bindingReview: Mammary preparation distinguished from postbirth synthesis and ejection.

items.title: Locate fertilization
items.guide: Mark a uterine/Fallopian tube, commonly its ampullary region, rather than the uterine lining. Label the ovary, tube and uterus to show why the fertilization location differs from the implantation surface.
items.bindingReview: Tube is usual fertilization location, uterus is implantation; diagram must show both.

items.title: Complete a hormone source-target table
items.guide: Use separate rows. Testosterone: interstitial cells → responsive reproductive and other tissues → support of reproductive function and secondary traits. GnRH: hypothalamus → anterior pituitary → FSH/LH release. Progesterone: corpus luteum and later placenta → endometrium and feedback centres → lining support and reduced upstream stimulation in the stated context. Estrogen: follicles and later placental production → responsive reproductive tissues/endometrium → growth and rebuilding, with feedback depending on cycle stage. FSH: anterior pituitary → Sertoli/follicular cells → support of germ-cell development. LH: anterior pituitary → interstitial cells or ovarian tissues → testosterone release or ovulation/luteal function. Correct the source composite row by separating FSH and LH.
items.bindingReview: All source-table rows now completed including target and response; FSH and LH composite separated.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: The final source-table entry combines gonadotropins; separate FSH and LH targets in your response.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: Testosterone: interstitial cells → responsive reproductive/other tissues. GnRH: hypothalamus → anterior pituitary, promoting FSH/LH. Progesterone: corpus luteum/placenta → endometrium and feedback centres. Estrogen: ovarian follicles and other specified sources → reproductive tissues/endometrium. FSH and LH are pituitary gonadotropins with different gonadal targets; the last composite row should not imply a single undifferentiated action.

items.title: Explain development signals
items.guide: In a typical pathway, Y-linked testis-development signalling leads to testes; testicular signals then influence reproductive ducts and external structures. Testosterone needs responsive targets. Development without those testicular signals follows different pathways. Chromosomes, signals and receptor response are separate pieces of evidence.
items.bindingReview: Gonadal developmental signals and receptor action mediate typical chromosome pathways rather than deterministic chromosome-only claims.

items.title: Compare gamete movement
items.guide: Sperm movement involves ductal contractions and later flagellar movement through reproductive fluids. The oocyte is received by the uterine tube and moved by cilia and smooth-muscle activity. It does not swim with a sperm-like flagellum. The mechanisms bring gametes toward the same region.
items.bindingReview: Muscular duct transport/flagellar movement versus tubal cilia/muscle; meeting region is common but propulsion differs.

items.title: Connect hormones to processes
items.guide: Fertilization depends on prior hormone-supported gamete production/ovulation rather than one hormone directly joining chromosomes. Early hCG supports the corpus luteum and progesterone while placental support develops. Prostaglandins and oxytocin contribute to labour. For each example, state the indirect or direct target action.
items.bindingReview: Hormones support prerequisites rather than directly fusing gametes; placental-stage and labour roles differentiated.

items.title: Draw ovarian feedback
items.guide: Show hypothalamus GnRH → pituitary FSH/LH → ovarian tissues → estrogen/progesterone. Add mainly negative-feedback arrows and the sustained-high-estrogen positive-feedback context leading to the LH surge. Label source, target and sign; do not draw a permanent positive-feedback loop throughout the cycle.
items.bindingReview: Both signs on the feedback loop, sustained-estrogen context before LH surge, no permanent positive loop.

items.title: Build an early-development timeline
items.guide: Nine events in sequence are fertilization, early cleavage, formation of a morula, organization of a blastocyst, implantation, gastrulation, neural-tube formation, early heart/blood-vessel development, and limb/organ patterning. Several overlap. The first eight weeks after fertilization establish many organ rudiments; this does not mean every organ is mature or fully functional.
items.bindingReview: Nine distinct early events counted against request for at least eight; eight-week boundary does not imply mature organ function.

revisionHistory.reason: Second source-question review completed missing requested operations or removed unsupported specificity.
revisionHistory.previousGuide: A valid sequence includes fertilization, cleavage, morula, blastocyst, implantation, gastrulation, early neural/heart development and limb/organ patterning. The first eight weeks after fertilization establish many organ rudiments; organs are not all mature or fully functional at that point.

items.title: Connect gamete structure to role
items.guide: Both gametes normally contribute one chromosome set. Sperm emphasize delivery, movement and interaction with coverings; the oocyte retains cytoplasm, organelles and resources for early development. Shared genetic contribution does not require identical cell size or structure.
items.bindingReview: Both haploid genetic contributions with asymmetric delivery/cytoplasmic roles, not genetically identical gametes.

items.title: Qualify the undescended-testis claim
items.guide: A warmer environment can impair spermatogenesis, so undescended testes can increase later reproductive risks. The source’s wording that this always “causes sterility” is too absolute. Severity, duration and other factors matter; the mechanism supports increased risk rather than a universal diagnosis.
items.bindingReview: Temperature-related production risk explains source idea without endorsing always-sterile assertion.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Replace the absolute sterility claim with a qualified mechanism and evidence requirement.

items.title: Compare amniote support structures
items.guide: A shelled amniote egg has amnion, chorion, yolk sac and allantois with roles in protection, gas exchange, nutrients and waste handling. Compare homologous structures while explaining that humans use a placenta and do not retain every egg function unchanged.
items.bindingReview: Amniote homology predicts four membranes; optional egg-specific functions are introduced before comparison.
items.preAttemptContext: In a shelled amniote egg, the amnion encloses protective fluid, chorionic surfaces support gas exchange, the yolk sac surrounds nutrient reserves, and the allantois has waste-handling and gas-exchange roles. Compare these roles with the human support structures already taught; the structures do not retain every function unchanged.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Correct chromosome-number wording
items.guide: Correct the printed question: a typical human gamete has 23 chromosomes, not 23 pairs. Fertilization combines two haploid sets into 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). Meiotic reduction prevents chromosome number from doubling each generation.
items.bindingReview: Printed 23 pairs corrected to 23 chromosomes; combining haploid sets restores diploid count.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Correct the source wording: a normal human gamete has 23 chromosomes, not 23 pairs.

items.title: Explain corpus-luteum alternatives
items.guide: After implantation, early hCG maintains corpus-luteum progesterone and estrogen secretion until placental production is established. Without that support, the corpus luteum regresses, steroid levels fall and menstruation follows. Fertilization alone and successful implantation are not interchangeable conditions.
items.bindingReview: Implantation/hCG maintains luteal steroids versus regression/withdrawal; fertilization alone not enough.

items.title: Separate reproductive and social roles
items.guide: The example can distinguish sperm donor, oocyte donor, gestational carrier and two intended/social parents. These roles can overlap and do not establish a universal legal definition of parenthood. A response should explain biological contributions and social/ethical considerations without ranking families.
items.bindingReview: Two gamete contributors, gestational support and social/intended parents can overlap; no legal ranking.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Separate biological contributions from social roles; the task does not supply a universal legal definition of parenthood.

items.title: Interpret an ovulation signal
items.guide: A marked LH rise is the strongest supplied signal that ovulation may be approaching in the model. The progesterone-related temperature rise usually follows ovulation; fertile cervical mucus is generally less thick and more penetrable. A single observation is not a personal fertility prediction.
items.bindingReview: LH surge is prospective signal; temperature rise usually retrospective and thick mucus not fertile pattern.
items.preAttemptContext: Optional background for the three observations: progesterone-related basal-temperature rise usually follows ovulation. Near the fertile interval, cervical mucus is generally less thick and more penetrable. The timing of a signal matters when deciding whether it predicts an approaching event or follows it.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Identify remaining androgen sources
items.guide: The testes are the main typical testosterone source, but adrenal tissues contribute androgen precursors and smaller androgen production can remain. Removing testes therefore greatly changes the hormone environment without making every androgen molecule vanish.
items.bindingReview: Testes are main typical source but adrenal androgen contributions remain; optional background makes alternative source explicit.
items.preAttemptContext: The adrenal glands are hormone-producing tissues above the kidneys. They contribute androgen precursors and smaller amounts of androgens, although testes are the main typical testosterone source. Removing one source need not remove every source.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Audit the unlabelled graph
items.guide: The vertical axis has no named variable or units, so the graph cannot uniquely identify a hormone or quantify risk. It shows a variable rising early and declining across development. A possible interpretation must be labelled a hypothesis and would need a named measure, units and source before it could serve as evidence.
items.bindingReview: Unlabelled vertical variable cannot uniquely identify a hormone or risk; interpretation must stay a hypothesis.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: The vertical axis lacks a variable and units. State the limitation before suggesting any interpretation.

items.title: Evaluate the limits of a fictional case
items.guide: Two possible explanations are disrupted ovulation and impaired passage through a uterine tube; apparently adequate semen does not test either pathway. Evidence of hormone-supported ovulation and separate evidence about tubal passage would distinguish them. A scientifically justified first action in this fictional case is to gather that evidence through appropriate professional assessment, rather than prescribe an exercise change from the person’s occupation. If a signalling problem is demonstrated, hormone support may address that step; IVF may bypass some transport barriers. State the demonstrated cause, limits, evidence and consent before comparing technologies; no method guarantees a birth.
items.bindingReview: Two causes, discriminating evidence, appropriate evidence-gathering first action and matching technologies now answer all three source operations.

revisionHistory.previousGuide: The case does not identify a cause: ovulatory, tubal and other factors are possibilities even with an apparently adequate semen assessment. State what evidence would distinguish them. Do not diagnose from occupation or prescribe a lifestyle change. A proposed technology must address a demonstrated pathway and be assessed with professional evidence and consent.

items.title: Use anatomical evidence cautiously
items.guide: Displacement/compression can contribute to more frequent urination, changed breathing comfort and digestive discomfort. Link each possibility to the bladder, diaphragm or digestive tract. The structural scenario suggests mechanisms, not a prediction that everyone will have the same symptoms.
items.bindingReview: Three mechanical possibilities linked to bladder, breathing and digestive displacement with variability.

items.title: Separate organ number from function
items.guide: One functioning ovary can still release oocytes and provide hormones, so pregnancy can remain possible if the other necessary pathways function. Removal of one ovary does not prove the remaining tube, uterus or endocrine system is functional; avoid a guarantee.
items.bindingReview: One functioning ovary may suffice only if other needed pathways work; count does not prove function.

items.title: Explain a vasectomy mechanism
items.guide: Interrupting the vas deferens blocks sperm transport. Sperm production can continue, with sperm broken down and reabsorbed. Accessory glands still supply most semen fluid. Transport interruption does not immediately establish absence of sperm in every later sample or remove hormone-producing tissue.
items.bindingReview: Vas interruption affects transport, not gland hormones or immediate sperm formation; fluid contribution can remain.

items.title: Compare FSH targets
items.guide: In testes, FSH acts on Sertoli cells to support sperm development. In ovaries, it supports follicular development and related estrogen production. The same pituitary hormone has different tissue targets; it is distinct from LH’s interstitial-cell and ovulation/luteal roles.
items.bindingReview: FSH acts via Sertoli versus follicular cells; LH roles not substituted.

items.title: Plan an evidence-based information outline
items.guide: Include what a teratogen is, exposure route/dose/timing, developmental vulnerability, evidence limitations and ways to seek reliable health information. Propose a placental-pathway visual and a clearly sourced developmental timeline. Avoid frightening deterministic images or personal blame; do not invent risk percentages.
items.bindingReview: Outline includes definition, dose/route/time/evidence; two proposed visuals are pathway and timeline, no invented risks.

items.title: Distinguish development from observation
items.guide: Reproductive structures develop over time, while ultrasound identification also depends on visibility, fetal position, equipment and timing. The printed timing is an approximate historical example, not proof that earlier identification is impossible. An image of anatomy does not establish every chromosome, hormone, identity or later characteristic.
items.bindingReview: Development and imaging visibility distinguished; source age window is not absolute and anatomy not full sex evidence.

items.title: Distinguish menstrual contexts
items.guide: Pregnancy, lactation and menopause can be associated with absence of menstruation through different endocrine contexts. A missing period alone does not identify the cause. Treat the textbook’s clinical age/diagnostic wording as historical, not a classroom diagnostic checklist.
items.bindingReview: Three contexts named; lactation mechanism introduced before optional task and no diagnostic threshold adopted.
items.preAttemptContext: Optional background: suckling can suppress the hypothalamic–pituitary signals supporting ovarian cycling, with substantial variation. Pregnancy, lactation and menopause involve different endocrine contexts; absent menstruation alone does not identify which applies.
items.preAttemptContextPolicy: Visible optional reinforcement background before the attempt; does not count as required core or replace required-course teaching.

items.title: Read a pregnancy case with limits
items.guide: Early pregnancy depends on corpus-luteum support before placental steroid production is established, so preserving ovarian support could be one biological consideration. The case does not provide the clinician’s complete decision process; timing alone cannot prove why a particular procedure was delayed.
items.bindingReview: Early luteal support is a plausible consideration, not an invented clinician decision.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Use only listed observations; the source does not supply a clinician’s reason for a missing measurement.

items.title: Distinguish unmeasured from unnecessary
items.guide: Several relevant signals, including LH, hCG and oxytocin, are absent from the listed table. Their roles differ by timing and process. A table’s omission does not establish that measuring one was unnecessary, so identify a relevant missing signal and explain its role without inventing the clinician’s reason.
items.bindingReview: Missing relevant hormone can be named, but omission cannot prove testing was unnecessary.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: An omitted hormone measurement does not establish why it was omitted.

items.title: Compare FSH values correctly
items.guide: Patient FSH changes from 6.1 IU/L at 37 weeks to below 4 at eight hours postpartum, 5.9 at four days, 31.4 at five weeks and 68.0 at two months. At five weeks, controls range from 0.9–6.9 IU/L; at two months, 1.2–8.1 IU/L. The patient therefore shows a large later rise and exceeds both supplied control ranges, which substantially overlap each other. Loss of ovarian negative feedback is a plausible mechanism. Control FSH at term was not measured and no early-postpartum control values are given, so a complete patient-versus-control time trajectory cannot be calculated.
items.bindingReview: All five patient FSH values and two control ranges independently read; term control is NM, not zero, and overlapping later controls are not a full time series.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: A control value marked not measured cannot be used as a numeric comparator.

items.title: Interpret hormone replacement cautiously
items.guide: After removal of ovaries and delivery of the placenta, major reproductive steroid sources are lost. Hormone replacement could address effects of reduced ovarian hormone production. The case supports that general rationale, but it does not supply enough information to justify a specific regimen or the exact timing.
items.bindingReview: Lost major steroid sources explain general rationale; data cannot justify an exact regimen or timing.
items.preAttemptSourceNotice: Explain the general missing hormone source; the supplied case cannot justify a specific treatment or exact timing.

items.title: Identify placental hormone support
items.guide: By late gestation, placental steroid production can maintain substantial estrogen despite removed ovaries, using appropriate precursors from the maternal–fetal system. Thus similar late-pregnancy estrogen values do not prove that the ovaries were still present or that every hormone source was unchanged.
items.bindingReview: Placental steroid production explains late estrogen despite absent ovaries; precursors and stage noted.

items.title: Connect birth and lactation pathways
items.guide: The placenta supported later pregnancy, while pituitary oxytocin/prolactin pathways were not removed with the ovaries. Labour and delivery depend on interacting signals, and after placental delivery changing steroid levels permit milk synthesis while oxytocin supports ejection. These facts explain a possible outcome rather than a guarantee for all cases.
items.bindingReview: Later placenta and intact pituitary pathways explain possible birth/lactation; ovaries are not the source of prolactin or oxytocin.
